summary: Report No. 31 of South Korean Interim Government Activities (USAMGIK), prepared by the National Economic Board, covers April 1948, the month before the 10 May election. It records 94% voter registration (7,730,000), 939-942 candidates for 200 seats, communist sabotage and the Cheju revolt, and the Pyongyang North-South conference rejected by American authorities. Economic sections show higher industrial and anthracite output, stable prices, a trade balance turning to export surplus, record rail freight, rising deposits and a revenue surplus. Political chapters cover KILA's de facto dissolution, amnesty for 3,000 political prisoners, police reform, the draft civil code and land sales. Vested-property policy, refugee flow of 15,848, Korean schools in Japan, youth and women's organizations and literacy gains are also documented. Historians will find dense tables, official framing of the election period and detailed reporting on Property Custody and agrarian reform.
highlights: About 7,730,000 voters, over 94 percent of those eligible, registered for the 10 May election by 9 April despite communist terror, with 939-942 candidates contesting 200 seats; about 52 of 13,455 registration booths were attacked.
The Pyongyang North-South conference opened 19 April; Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic attended, and a 30 April communique rejected the South-only election, which the report judged a Soviet victory.
Cheju-do revolt broke out from 3 April with about 2,000 rioters; to 19 April, 22 civilians and seven police were killed, and 16 telephone poles and 26 wires were cut there.

KILA met once on 19 April and adjourned for 30 days, effectively dissolving itself after 11 Public Acts; an amnesty freed about 3,000 political prisoners and police now needed court warrants for arrests.
Anthracite output rose 49.5 percent to 62,796 tons, 40,596 of it from the Samchuk mine, while Japanese bituminous imports reached 83,171 tons and railroads carried a record 480,000 tons of freight.
By 30 April, 168,735 of 587,974 former Japanese farms (28.7 percent) had been sold to Korean farmers under Ordinance No. 173, and fertilizer sales through KAA reached 35,091 tons.
April licenses showed exports of 443.8 million won exceeding imports of 376.8 million by about 15 percent, against a 1,000 percent import excess a year earlier.
Refugee entries from North Korea reached 15,848, up 20 percent on March, while Korean schools in Japan were closed, leading to 73 parent arrests in Hyogo on 15 April.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover of Report No. 31 (April 1948) by the National Economic Board, a map, USAMGIK and SKIG organization charts as of 1 January 1948, the NEB roster under Dr. Wilhelm Anderson, and a six-part contents.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: Thirteen paragraphs: 7,730,000 voters (94 percent) registered for the 10 May election despite communist terror; Cheju revolt; Pyongyang conference; over 15,000 refugees; 28 percent of farmland sold; literacy up from 21 to 71 percent.

sections.title: Part I: Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Refugee inflow of 15,848 from North Korea, Korean League and school disputes in Japan, and Office of Property Custody work: 895 financial forms, 96 sales worth 62.4 million won, 102,822 leases.

sections.title: Section 1: Population and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: Refugee inflow rose 20 percent over March; the Korean League in Japan expelled dissenters; Osaka and Hyogo clashes over closure of non-conforming Korean schools led to 73 arrests on 15 April.

sections.title: Population Migration
sections.summary: April refugee entries from North Korea were 15,848, up 20 percent over March, as Russians tightened travel limits. The Kaesong camp was inspected 19 April; cumulative inbound total was 2,384,553 against 886,203 outbound.

sections.title: Korean League in Japan
sections.summary: A minority in the Korean League in Japan trying to end communist domination was defeated and expelled by leftist leaders, according to the Office of Foreign Affairs; dissenters formed separate political groups.

sections.title: Korean Education in Japan
sections.summary: Osaka ordered 19 non-compliant Korean schools closed by 15 April and 14 kept teaching. In Hyogo, 73 parents were arrested on 15 April and about 4,000 protesters dispersed on 18 April.

sections.title: Section 2: Vested Property
sections.summary: Office of Property Custody work: Form 20 and 21 financial statements, guaranteed loans, rules for selling small businesses and residences, an expedited claims procedure, audits and rental statistics.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Operations centered on Forms 20 and 21 financial statements from supervised industries, and standard rules for disposing of vested property were widely published. Policy memoranda were issued and 21 chemical plants inspected.

sections.title: Operations
sections.summary: Operations received 895 financial forms, 519 tabulated showing a net loss of 389.5 million won before taxes. Inspections found 21 chemical plants under 30 percent capacity; 51 loan cases totaling 2,138 million won were tabulated.

sections.title: Property Disposal
sections.summary: Rules for selling Japanese small businesses and residences give managers or occupants first chance, require 20 percent down, 5-7 percent interest and contracts up to 10 years. April sales completed: 96, worth 62.4 million won.

sections.title: Real Estate Section
sections.summary: The Real Estate Section handled 19 transfers of Army-released property, including six covering 180 Seoul houses, processed 21 Army requisitions, and planned transfer of Army real property to the Korean government should USAFIK withdraw.

sections.title: Policies and Precedents
sections.summary: A statement held that property registered to Allied nationals on 9 August 1945 is not vested but is protected by the Custodian. Further papers addressed ending brothel use of vested properties and barring lease of critical industrial assets.

sections.title: Claims Section
sections.summary: On 17 April the Military Governor signed a directive simplifying ownership claims against vested property. Only 50 of over 50,000 Ordinance No. 33 claims were processed in a year; the new eight-step procedure reached 12 cases a day.

sections.title: Audit Division
sections.summary: The Audit Division completed audits of seven organizations and five investigation reports; 52 of 922 requested desk audits were done. Audit work was decentralized to provincial offices, with balance-sheet audits replacing detailed ones.

sections.title: Property Rentals
sections.summary: As of 1 January 1948 there were 102,822 leases on 82,339 properties; 21.4 percent were delinquent (87.2 million won). Gross collections since liberation were 319.3 million won, net 283.5 million; residences numbered 56,080.

sections.title: Part II: Production and Supply
sections.summary: Agriculture, prices, industry, mining, allocation, trade and labor: fertilizer sales of 35,091 tons, 28.7 percent of vested farms sold, anthracite at 62,796 tons, exports exceeding imports, and a Seoul Electric strike threat.

sections.title: Section 1: Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries
sections.summary: Fertilizer sales through KAA reached 35,091 tons; 168,735 vested farms were sold; Crop Reporting Service staff reached 664; livestock, silk, forestry and fisheries are also reported.

sections.title: Agricultural Economics Bureau
sections.summary: The Crop Reporting Service added 281 persons, bringing appointments to 664 as of 20 April. Gun statistician training began in Kyonggi-do, and a grain inspectors' school at Yongdungpo graduated 200.

sections.title: Agriculture Production Bureau
sections.summary: Livestock numbers rose from 1946. The Seoul milk plant lost 30 percent of its milk for lack of ammonia. USGS arranged 400 tons each of sulphur and copper sulphate from Japan; exportable silk graded poorly.

sections.title: Bureau of Forestry
sections.summary: Forest output for January and February 1948 was 39,660 and 36,092 cubic meters of logs. Seoul fuelwood fell from 4,000 to 2,500 won per cubic meter, and nurseries received 222 tons of ammonium nitrate.

sections.title: Bureau of Fisheries
sections.summary: Processed marine products for 1947 were 54,870 metric tons, 3,736 below 1946, blamed on shortages of tinplate, salt and transport. A 14-vessel deep-sea expedition from Pusan landed 389 tons.

sections.title: Korea Agricultural Association
sections.summary: KAA imported 38,464 tons of fertilizer and sold 35,091 in April; since July, 306,895 tons were received and 75 percent sold. KAA collected 839.7 million won and bought 22.2 million straw bags.

sections.title: Agricultural Improvement Service
sections.summary: The service investigated unexplained fees levied by 20 organizations in the two Kyongsang provinces. Maj.-Gen. Dean said AIS would unify research, teaching and extension; extension agents agreed to use village discussion clubs.

sections.title: National Land Administration
sections.summary: Under Ordinance No. 173, 168,735 of 587,974 former Japanese farms (28.7 percent) were sold by 30 April. Buyers were capped at two chungbo, price was three times annual output, paid at 20 percent of crop for 15 years.

sections.title: Section 2: Prices
sections.summary: Retail prices in Seoul and nine cities eased seasonally in April while wholesale prices were nearly unchanged; Seoul rice retailed at 1,320 won per mal, and controlled price lists were published.

sections.title: Retail and Wholesale Prices
sections.summary: Retail prices slipped seasonally except Korean turnip, salt, cotton shirting and briquettes. Wholesale dried fish, hemp, lumber, cement and coal rose, while cleaned rice, cotton yarn and copper fell. Seoul rice: 1,320 won per mal.

sections.title: Controlled Prices
sections.summary: The National Price Administration's March 1948 schedule listed controlled prices, such as cleaned rice at 280 won per large mal, cotton sheeting 56 won per yard, lump anthracite 3,500 won per ton and calf leather shoes 1,660 won.

sections.title: Section 3: Industrial Production
sections.summary: March output rose sharply: cotton yarn 28.5 percent, cloth 26.2 percent, paper 36.1 percent, nails 19.3 percent and oxygen 80 percent; salt output and cigarette shortfalls from the Monopoly Bureau are also reported.

sections.title: Processed Food
sections.summary: The Taihan mill and six small mills made 2,386 tons of flour in March, 3.1 percent above February. Six of nine small mills made 628 tons; noodle output was 77 tons.

sections.title: Textiles
sections.summary: Cotton yarn rose 28.5 percent to 522,000 kg, the best since June 1947; cotton cloth rose 26.2 percent to 2,286,000 meters despite power shortages, one mill getting 300 KW daily against 1,000 KW needed.

sections.title: Paper
sections.summary: Machine-made paper from 14 mills hit a post-liberation record of 533.4 metric tons in March, against 391.9 in February. Puksun exceeded its best Japanese-era month by 16 percent.

sections.title: Hardware
sections.summary: Nail production in March was 148.9 metric tons, 19.3 percent above February's 124.8 and near the 1947 monthly average of 142.1, from three South Korean plants.

sections.title: Chemicals
sections.summary: Briquettes rose 41.3 percent to 6,398 tons, under a third of March 1947, for lack of pitch. Rubber shoes reached 1,899,834 pairs, oxygen 90,455 cubic meters, and common brick resumed at 10,000 tons.

sections.title: Miscellaneous
sections.summary: Electric insulators fell to 5,512 pieces from 11,760 in February because coal was scarce, while lead pencils rose to 4,521 gross from 3,684.

sections.title: Monopoly Bureau Products
sections.summary: Government salterns produced 16,036 tons in April, nearly triple April 1947. Cigarette output fell 17.6 percent to 288.8 tons after a week's shutdown for lack of endless tape; cut tobacco rose to 686.6 tons.

sections.title: Section 4: Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: Anthracite output jumped 49.5 percent to 62,796 tons, mostly from the Samchuk mine; bituminous imports from Japan were 83,171 tons; pitch shortage cut briquettes; gold and other mineral output are tabulated.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Coal rehabilitation was beginning to meet its goal: anthracite output expanded sharply in March and April Japanese bituminous imports nearly matched February's record, nearly doubling coal supply versus three months earlier.

sections.title: Indigenous Anthracite and Lignite Coal
sections.summary: Anthracite rose 49.5 percent to 62,796 tons, 40,596 from Samchuk; lignite reached 5,112 tons. Under half reached market, with 53,000 tons stranded at railheads. Yong Wol made 10,250 tons in April.

sections.title: Bituminous Coal
sections.summary: Bituminous imports from Japan, the only source, were 83,171 tons in April against February's record 83,330. Railroads received 58,150 tons but needed at least 100,000 monthly.

sections.title: Shipments to Consumers
sections.summary: Deliveries to consumers lagged production and imports because of pilferage and transport limits. In March 36,659 tons of anthracite and 51,983 tons of bituminous coal were actually supplied.

sections.title: Pitch
sections.summary: Coal tar pitch, the binder for briquettes, was virtually unavailable in March, holding briquettes to about one-third of the 1947 average. Pitch ordered from the United States was not expected for two months.

sections.title: Other Minerals
sections.summary: Five Bureau of Mining teams visited over 30 vested gold properties and found 683 stamps in 70 mills yielding about 20,000 grams monthly with 3,500 miners. Kobayashi Mining planned 10 tons monthly of ferro-tungsten.

sections.title: Section 5: Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: Consumer Goods Allocation Board procedure, civilian supply allocations, April petroleum allocations (6,414,345 liters gasoline), salt distribution of 25,803 tons, and allocation of Korean-produced commodities.

sections.title: Consumer Goods Allocation Board
sections.summary: The National Consumer Goods Office distributed its Standard Operating Procedure summarizing Executive Order No. 12. G-4, XXIV Corps agreed incentive goods go to unit commanders where employee co-operatives exist.

sections.title: Allocation of Civilian Supplies
sections.summary: Miscellaneous Pusan supplies would be priced against inventory and reconciled later with shipping documents, easing Yongdungpo congestion. April allocations included 4,555 bales raw cotton, 1,500 tons rubber and 78,980 bags cement.

sections.title: Petroleum
sections.summary: April allocations were 6,414,345 liters gasoline, 3,815,507 kerosene, 2,924,821 diesel and 4,242,796 Navy Special fuel oil. An anti-illegal-sales ordinance was drafted and the Inchon pipeline to Wangemiri neared completion.

sections.title: Salt Distribution
sections.summary: The Monopoly Bureau distributed 25,803 metric tons of salt in April, with 60,812,947 kg in stock for May. Soya-sauce rations took 21,169,282 kg and fisheries curing 3,268,020 kg.

sections.title: Allocation of Korean-Produced Commodities
sections.summary: On 15 April the Board unanimously set a 40 percent share for government and vested-industry employees and 60 percent for the public, up from 30-70. April allocations totaled 766,082 thousand won across 446 allocations.

sections.title: Distribution of Korean-Produced Commodities
sections.summary: The 1947 year-end bonus distribution bought 41,000,000 won of goods, 96 percent of the allocation. The FFA contract was completed 23 April: FFA receives 15 percent, pays FDA eight, retailers earn 13; 462,505 employees were eligible.

sections.title: Section 6: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: April licenses show exports of 443.8 million won exceeding imports of 376.8 million by about 15 percent, against a 1,000 percent import excess a year earlier; Hong Kong took over 93 percent of exports.

sections.title: Private Trade Statistics
sections.summary: April licenses (113 import, 94 export) indicate exports of 443.8 million won against imports of 376.8 million. March imports were 822.7 million won and exports 654.1 million; Hong Kong took over 93 percent of exports.

sections.title: Private Trade Activities
sections.summary: April trade with Hong Kong was carried by vessels including the Suchow, which took 500 tons of exports. Arrivals at Pusan and Inchon included paraffin wax, caustic soda, rubber and 213 tons of wool.

sections.title: Government-to-Government Transactions
sections.summary: Exports to Japan credited to the USAMGIK account were $351,976 for April and $4,223,237 for January-April. SCAP's offer of six cents per pound for hemp waste was accepted; 75 tons of lead bullion was offered to a New York firm.

sections.title: Korean Items for Americans in Korea
sections.summary: Sales of Korean-made goods to the Army Exchange Service were $27,355 in April, bringing the total since August 1947 to $174,506. April deliveries were 17,434 pieces.

sections.title: Civilian Supply Imports
sections.summary: April imports included 83,171 metric tons of coal, 47,815 tons of fertilizer with a record 15,551 tons of ammonium sulphate from Japan, rice (6,226 tons from the U.S.) and 19,515 tons of salt.

sections.title: Section 7: Labor
sections.summary: A May Day permit dispute, a threatened Seoul Electric streetcar strike, labor law enforcement, labor education, industrial health and abandonment of the labor distribution project at refugee camps.

sections.title: Labor Union Activities
sections.summary: Chung Pyung's May Day permit complaint went to General Dean, who warned against an illegal Seoul Electric strike and named an eight-member fact-finding committee. Tai Han won 366 of 413 votes.

sections.title: Labor Laws
sections.summary: Samchok mines were found to have violated the Maximum Working Hours Law (Ordinance No. 121) until September 1947. Seoul ration stores were exempted from the 60-hour limit during the election; minors under 14 in government offices were dismissed.

sections.title: Labor Education
sections.summary: The Bureau of Labor Relations showed an exhibit on American labor, planned educational tours to six towns in Kangwon-do and Chungchong-pukto, circulated 7,500 copies of Labor News and aired four Laborers' Hour broadcasts.

sections.title: Industrial Health
sections.summary: Industrial health teams gave 6,615 immunizations at five Seoul firms and 43,969 at Kangwon-do mines, where they found poor hospitals, spoiled meat, silicosis and tuberculosis. A recreation program began for 200 girl workers.

sections.title: Labor Distribution
sections.summary: Special labor officers were withdrawn from refugee camps at Uijongbu and Kaesong. Of 424 workers distributed during 1947 only 60 proved skilled, so the project was abandoned.

sections.title: Part III: Public Services
sections.summary: Transportation (record rail freight over 480,000 tons), communications (Cheju sabotage, new stamps), utilities (75.9 million KWH, power barges) and public works (volunteer labor, 144 fires).

sections.title: Section 1: Transportation
sections.summary: A 60-day shipping priority system was adopted; March Transportation revenue rose 119 percent; railroads carried over 480,000 tons of freight, the most since October 1945.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: The Department of Transportation set a 60-day cargo priority system: 48 percent for Pusan allotments, 24 coal, 19 rice, six fertilizer from Yosu and three miscellaneous.

sections.title: Revenue and Expenditures
sections.summary: March revenue rose 119 percent, or 283,000,000 won, the highest of F/Y 1947/48, including 161,000,000 won from the U.S. Army. Revenue was 520,065 thousand won against expenditures of 464,552 thousand.

sections.title: Railroads
sections.summary: Anti-sabotage precautions kept April damage small. March rail receipts rose 269,000,000 won, passengers by 921,000, and freight passed 480,000 tons, the most since October 1945. Operable locomotives rose by 17.

sections.title: Marine Transportation
sections.summary: Marine receipts for March were 147 percent above February. Employment rose to 2,540. Dredging let FS-type ships enter Pohang, continued at Kunsan and Mokpo, and wreckage removal began at Yosu.

sections.title: Highway and Air Transportation
sections.summary: Highway expenditures fell to 356 thousand won in March while air outlays rose nine percent to 296 thousand. Neither reported income; employment was 72 on highways and 31 in air transport.

sections.title: Section 2: Communications
sections.summary: Communist sabotage shifted to Cheju, where 16 poles and 26 wires were cut; March revenue, employment (13,113), postal savings, telephone, telegraph, radio fees, and two new stamps are reported.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Sabotage on the mainland waned but hit Cheju island: 16 telephone poles cut and 26 wires severed. In Kwangju, telephone and telegraph employees rioted, partly interrupting service for over 24 hours.

sections.title: Revenue and Expenditures
sections.summary: March revenue rose markedly: telephone fees up 14,000,000 won, insurance 2,000,000 and stamps 1,000,000. Expenditures dropped over 50 percent to 39,282 thousand won for lack of year-end funds.

sections.title: Employment
sections.summary: Department of Communications employment fell to 13,113 in March from 13,479, under Military Governor reduction orders. Postal staff numbered 3,292, insurance 871 and telephone 3,068.

sections.title: Special Functions
sections.summary: Communications collected 726 million won for Finance in March, up over 39 percent and the highest since October 1945, with taxes at 704 million won and cigarette factories running the full month.

sections.title: Postal Deposits and Insurance
sections.summary: Postal deposits held at 843 million won with 7,002 thousand depositors; transfer deposits were 154 million won. National Life Insurance in force rose 6,000,000 won to 1,776 million.

sections.title: Telephone and Telegraph
sections.summary: March telephone messages were 182,000, up 17,000, with revenue of 11,464 thousand won. Domestic telegrams numbered 182,215, earning 6,691,343 won.

sections.title: Korean Broadcasting Corporation
sections.summary: Effective 15 April, the radio license fee for Korean civilian owners of entertainment receivers rose from 40 won to 50 won per month.

sections.title: Communications Bureau
sections.summary: The Korean Electric Power Company's Seoul-Pusan telephone circuit was re-aligned 20 April. Inspections of three Seoul plants surveyed capacity for telephone parts and 20 constabulary radio transmitters.

sections.title: Postal Bureau
sections.summary: Two new stamps went on sale 10 April: a pink 20-won Independence Gate (one million printed) and a light brown 50-won Turtle Ship (500,000 printed).

sections.title: Section 3: Public Utilities
sections.summary: Electric power delivered in April was 75.9 million KWH, 33.7 million from southern sources; Emergency Power Board meetings, plant output, Seoul streetcars and the YFP-1 and Electra power barges.

sections.title: Electricity Distribution
sections.summary: April deliveries totaled 75,900,000 KWH, slightly below March, with 42.2 million from north of 38 degrees and 33.7 from the south. Compiled data on all South Korean plants since August 1945 were shown for the first time.

sections.title: Emergency Power Board Transactions
sections.summary: The Board met 7 and 21 April on allocation if North Korean power were cut. Unauthorized uses were estimated at 30 percent of supply. Adviser Roames outlined load dispatching and three 5,000 KVA transformers from Japan.

sections.title: Power Plants
sections.summary: Chung Pyung hydro averaged 15,700 KW, Sumjingang 8,700 KW, Yong Wol steam 7,200 KW, and the Pusan floating plant about 6,500 KW. Tests showed Dong In Ri can generate 18,000 KW continuously.

sections.title: Street Railways
sections.summary: Seoul streetcars ran about 135 cars. Fred Simons's study settled a dispute over 27,909,000 won in claimed taxes owed by Seoul Electric: vehicle and rail taxes due in installments, traffic tax invalid.

sections.title: Auxiliary Power Barges
sections.summary: The 20,000 KW barge YFP-1 was berthed at Pusan and began producing at once, the first floating plant of its kind. The Navy barge Electra, with six 800 KW generators, reached Inchon.

sections.title: Section 4: Public Works
sections.summary: No national road appropriation existed, so volunteer labor carried road, bridge, levee and fire-control work after a detailed spring inspection; April saw 144 fires and the Heavy Equipment School graduated 86.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: April brought the most detailed inspection of Public Works sites yet, showing progress despite funding shortages. Volunteer labor on roads, bridges and irrigation increased and new volunteer fire companies were installed.

sections.title: Highways
sections.summary: Highway employment and spending were nearly nil without a national appropriation. Surveys covered 54 km of the planned Seoul-east coast highway, the Kangnung-Samchok mine road and the Yongwol-Chungju-Chochiwon road.

sections.title: Bridges
sections.summary: The Andong bridge was 20 percent complete at 4,478 thousand won, and a contract was let 22 April for the Waegwan bridge deck. Capt. Nelson's Namjong Bridge redesign saves 5,000 bags of cement and 3,500,500 won.

sections.title: Irrigation and Flood Control
sections.summary: A Water Resources Committee under Choi Kyong-wol met 2 and 23 April and began reviewing the Sum Jin Gang dam. A flood report cited 311 rivers and 1,250,000 feet of needed levees.

sections.title: Urban Water Supply
sections.summary: The City Planning Bureau drew up the 1948/49 water works program. Power failures were the main problem, and the Utilities Commission approved Seoul rate increases up to 80 times 1937 levels, about 25 won per seven cubic meters.

sections.title: Maps and Surveys
sections.summary: The Bureau of Geodetic Survey studied the accuracy of the 1:50,000 maps and compiled all triangulation points. The pages also hold flood control programs (4,866 million won to complete, 69,500 hectares).

sections.title: Fire Control
sections.summary: April saw 144 fires with 76,018,490 won in losses, one-fifth of March's; January-April totaled 693 fires. All but five of Seoul's 32 fire lanes were passable, and a firm produced 1,200 yards of hose.

sections.title: Education
sections.summary: On 3 April the Heavy Equipment School at Ascom City graduated its second class of 86 Korean engineers after a three-month course, 12 February to 3 April.

sections.title: Part IV: Finance
sections.summary: Government finance (note issue down 5,213 million won from December's 33,389 million, overdraft 22,005 million, budget 23,370 million) and non-government finance (deposits 55,305 million, loans 32,120 million).

sections.title: Section 1: Government Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun note issue fell 5,213 million won from December's 33,389 million; cumulative overdraft hit 22,005 million; March revenue set a record of 2,135 million won.

sections.title: Note Issue of the Bank of Chosun
sections.summary: Note issue peaked at 33,389 million won in December 1947 and fell 5,213 million by end of April, owing to completed rice collection, record tax collections and tobacco sales, and 1,132 million won of deposit transfers.

sections.title: Overdraft to South Korean Interim Government
sections.summary: Cumulative excess withdrawals reached a new high of 22,005 million won at end of April. April withdrawals were 2,340 million against 1,555 million deposits; total overdrafts were 39,325 million.

sections.title: Expenditure Budget of the South Korean Interim Government
sections.summary: The approved F/Y 1947/48 budget of 21,407 million won, with 787,000,000 added and 1,177 million pending, totals 23,370 million. The 1948/49 recommendation is 28,704,824 thousand won expenditure against 27,821,485 thousand revenue.

sections.title: Monthly Revenues and Expenditures
sections.summary: March revenues of 2,135 million won set a monthly record, 507 million above February. Monopoly Bureau receipts were 1,004 million won, taxes 432 million; expenditures rose 601 million over February.

sections.title: Ratios Between Revenues and Expenditures
sections.summary: Cumulative F/Y 1947/48 revenue of 15,336 million won, led by the Monopoly Bureau at 7,294 million, was 79 percent of expenditure payments of 19,319 million.

sections.title: Monopoly Bureau
sections.summary: Monopoly Bureau March expenditures were 195.5 million won and fiscal year 3,539 million, mostly tobacco (2,698 million). Year revenue was 7,294 million; tobacco supplies 36 percent of estimated revenue.

sections.title: Civilian Supply Program
sections.summary: The Civilian Supply Program sells goods bought from Japan and the United States through SKIG channels. The balance stood at 5,319 million won at end of April 1948, with 13,686 million in receivables.

sections.title: Section 2: Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: Deposits in financial institutions rose to a record 55,305 million won, loans fell to 32,120 million, cash balances rose to 3,508.9 million, and insurance and bank activities are reported.

sections.title: Cash Balances in Financial Institutions
sections.summary: Cash balances in financial institutions rose 1,088 million won in March to 3,508.9 million, partly a rebound from February's fall. South Korea has no securities markets and no legal liquid-reserve requirement.

sections.title: Deposits in Financial Institutions
sections.summary: Deposit balances rose 6,279 million won, nearly 13 percent, to a record 55,305 million in March. Government balances grew nearly 1,900 million to 28,926 million; inter-bank balances reached 4,151 million.

sections.title: Deposit Balances in Each Financial Institution
sections.summary: Public deposits rose 3,221 million won to a record 22,228 million, and every deposit type rose at every institution in March. Government deposits gained mainly at the Bank of Chosun; total balances were 55,305 million.

sections.title: Loans by Financial Institutions
sections.summary: March was the third straight month retirements exceeded new loans; outstanding loans fell 1,591 million won to 32,120 million. The Bank of Chosun held 30 percent; loans equalled 58 percent of deposits.

sections.title: Life Insurance
sections.summary: Insurance in force rose 74.4 million won, nine percent, to 814.6 million in March. Premiums collected were 68 percent above February; four companies reported.

sections.title: Damage Insurance
sections.summary: Companies wrote 9,265 new policies in March. Liabilities assumed of nearly 4,400 million won set a record, 42 percent above February, and premiums written reached 51.6 million.

sections.title: Life and Damage Insurance Activities
sections.summary: Damage insurers were told to limit investments to mortgages, real estate, bonds, stocks, deposits and Korean Government obligations. A new life insurance salary scale raised maximum salaries about 50 percent.

sections.title: Activities of Financial Institutions
sections.summary: The Bank Examination Section examined its first Korean bank. Controller of Commodities proposed repaying the 12,502 million won rice loan by 31 October. Ordinance 182 replaced 100 won notes; 39 loans totaling 713 million won were approved.

sections.title: Part V: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Election preparations (7,730,000 registered, 942 candidates), KILA's dissolution, the Pyongyang conference, Executive Order 20 moving the election to 10 May, police reform, Cheju violence and weekly North-South mail.

sections.title: Section 1: Administration
sections.summary: Registration closed 9 April with 7,730,000 voters and 942 candidates; the National Economic Board met seven times; Military Government personnel numbered 3,041.

sections.title: Preparation for National Election
sections.summary: Registration closed 9 April with 7,730,000 voters, over 94 percent of those eligible; 200 districts and 13,407 polling places were set and 942 candidates registered. Public Information ran 100 film shorts and radio coverage.

sections.title: National Economic Board
sections.summary: The NEB met seven times and reviewed F/Y 1948/49 budgets, authorised 400 million won credit for the Korean Irrigation Union, passed 250 million for the Sumjingang Dam, and approved summer grain collection of at least 20 percent.

sections.title: Military Government Personnel
sections.summary: Military Government personnel numbered 3,041 in April 1948 (547 officers, 1,469 enlisted men, 1,025 civilians), up from 2,740 in March; the total was 3,721 in October 1946.

sections.title: Section 2: Korean Interim Legislative Assembly
sections.summary: KILA met once, on 19 April, enacted nothing and adjourned for 30 days, tantamount to dissolution; its record was 11 Public Acts and four resolutions.

sections.title: April Session
sections.summary: KILA met only on 19 April and enacted no legislation. It rejected three resignations to keep membership at 49, tabled pending bills until the National Assembly convenes, and adjourned 30 days.

sections.title: Summary of KILA Legislation
sections.summary: KILA, convened 12 December 1946 with 45 elected and 45 appointed members, passed 11 Public Acts and four resolutions, and nearly dissolved three times: May 1947, November 1947 and January-February 1948.

sections.title: Section 3: Political Developments
sections.summary: The Pyongyang North-South conference from 19 April, which Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic attended, 939 candidates for 200 seats, and landlord and communist opposition to farmland sales.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: The Pyongyang conference opening 19 April and the first general election absorbed parties. Over 90 percent registered and 939 candidates sought 200 seats when registration closed 16 April.

sections.title: North-South Conference
sections.summary: Moderates and leftists backed the conference; the Hankook Democratic Party and Rhee opposed it. Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic went to Pyongyang. A 30 April communique rejected the separate election.

sections.title: Election Preparations
sections.summary: Rightists formed an acceleration committee under O Sei-chang; 939 candidates, 17 of them women, contested 200 seats, with Rhee's society fielding 239 and Dai Dong 89. Choi Nung-chin's challenge to Rhee was nullified 7 May.

sections.title: Land Reform
sections.summary: Extreme rightists, backed largely by landlords, opposed sale of New Korea Company land to tenants. Communists accused U.S. authorities of keeping proceeds and wanted free distribution as in North Korea.

sections.title: Section 4: Legal Affairs
sections.summary: Executive Order 20 moved the election to 10 May because of an eclipse; also Ordinances 182-191, Justice Department opinions, prison conditions, amnesty release, and Judge Lobingier's draft Civil Code.

sections.title: Ordinances and Orders
sections.summary: Executive Order 20 moved the election to 10 May because of an eclipse; Ordinances 182-191 raised the income tax exemption to 25,000 won. Hodge proclaimed 11 rights of Koreans on 5 April.

sections.title: Legal Opinions
sections.summary: Justice opinions held foreign firms such as Jardine, Matheson need no licence to trade, that English is official in the National Land Administration, and that the National Food Administration is independent of the NEB.

sections.title: Penal Institutions
sections.summary: Prisons were guarded against election-time release attempts. Kunchon Prison became an adult institution taking about 200 overflow prisoners. The Kaesong Boys' Reformatory held 1,100 boys aged 14 to 20.

sections.title: Court Liaison
sections.summary: Release of prisoners under the Military Governor's amnesty was completed in April except for some transferred prisoners being traced; many pardon-order copies could not be delivered for lack of addresses.

sections.title: Property Claims Commission
sections.summary: The Justice adviser and Property Custodian recommended transferring claims with abundant proof of Korean ownership to the Custodian, and the Commission concurred, speeding administrative release of property.

sections.title: Codification Bureau
sections.summary: Judge C. Sumner Lobingier's proposed Civil Code, Korea's first, was finished and being translated. It has four books: Persons, Obligations, Property and Succession.

sections.title: Section 5: National Police
sections.summary: The court-warrant rule worked better than expected; communist violence aimed at registration, attacking about 52 of 13,455 booths; Cheju-do rioting killed 22 civilians and seven police by 19 April.

sections.title: Reform Measures
sections.summary: The court-warrant requirement worked more smoothly than expected, though police felt they lost face when over 3,000 minor political offenders were released and resented limits on force.

sections.title: Violence
sections.summary: About 52 of 13,455 registration booths were attacked, led by Kyongsang-pukto with 21. Cheju-do's outbreak from 3 April involved about 2,000 rioters; 22 civilians and seven police were killed to 19 April.

sections.title: Warning
sections.summary: Communists were renewing efforts to win adherents among security forces, telling police the Americans were leaving and joining the winning side would be wise.

sections.title: Section 6: Interzone Activities
sections.summary: Weekly North-South mail exchange handled 59,000 pieces, Radio Pyongyang attacked the southern election, and 38th parallel incidents reached a new high with 21 Koreans killed since 7 February.

sections.title: Mail Exchange
sections.summary: Mail exchange became weekly from 15 April. Four exchanges handled 59,000 pieces versus 37,000 in March; the largest, on 3 April, carried 9,768 letters from South Korea.

sections.title: Radio Pyongyang Intercepts
sections.summary: Radio Pyongyang used the Joint Conference to attack the southern election and denounce Rhee. Kim Il-sung's opening speech was the key broadcast; the People's Assembly adopted a constitution 28-30 April.

sections.title: Border Incidents
sections.summary: Police Director Chough Pyong-ok said border incidents reached a new high, with Soviet soldiers accompanying raids. Since 7 February 21 Koreans were killed and about 150 wounded; marauders violated the border 74 times.

sections.title: Part VI: Social
sections.summary: Public health (cholera vaccine, Mukden repatriates), education (literacy from 21 to 71 percent), culture (Arbor Day, Olympic team), press, Korean National Youth (774,949 members) and women's activities.

sections.title: Section 1: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Welfare and medical teams sailed with the Mukden repatriate ship; cholera vaccine reached the provinces; nurse training began; 10,053 housing units were completed; lepers, narcotics and laboratories are covered.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Public Health outfitted the Mukden refugee ship with welfare and preventive medicine teams, began a graduate nurse program, and sent cholera vaccine to the provinces for three-phase vaccination.

sections.title: Preventive Medicine
sections.summary: Typhus and typhoid declined. The National Health Center milk station served 120 infants daily. The Mukden refugee ship sailed 30 April with a 14-day quarantine planned.

sections.title: Medical Services
sections.summary: The last UNRRA medical shipment, worth about $2,000, was divided among four leprosaria at Yosu, Sorakto, Taegu and Pusan. The tenth Lasan Sanitorium course finished, totalling 50 graduates.

sections.title: Nursing Affairs
sections.summary: A three-month graduate nurse program began 1 April at three U.S. Army hospitals under the 80th Medical Group. Pusan Transportation Hospital was found poor, Pusan City Hospital much improved.

sections.title: Veterinary Affairs
sections.summary: Cattle treated rose from 26,302 in 1946 to 34,591 in 1947, with 97 percent recoveries. The fifth veterinary bulletin on horse breeding was distributed, 560 copies in all.

sections.title: Pharmaceutical Affairs
sections.summary: Military Government received 520,000 pounds of DDT, distributed through Army Malaria Control Units, and the first 100,000 bars of soap. Only two of 44 pharmacist candidates completed all three exam parts.

sections.title: Narcotics Section
sections.summary: The Narcotics Section licensed 74 physicians and 31 pharmacists to handle narcotics, and inspected the narcotics ward at Sun Hwa Hospital, Seoul, interviewing six addicts.

sections.title: Laboratories
sections.summary: The National Vaccine Laboratory in Seoul met requirements and increased cholera, typhoid and rabies vaccine output; smallpox vaccine was delayed by budget difficulties.

sections.title: Public Assistance
sections.summary: A flood-season relief plan relies on local organizations. Welfare officers completed 10,053 low-cost housing units, five child welfare institutions were licensed, and the Kaesong camp processes 500 to 1,000 refugees.

sections.title: Section 2: Education
sections.summary: Adult literacy rose from 21 to 71 percent, curriculum workshops grew, South Korea's first model hospital ward was arranged, and each bureau reports activities including 13,230,670 textbooks published.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Curriculum workshops in art, music, science, home economics and English drew many teachers. The Medical Section arranged South Korea's first model hospital ward, and adult education greatly reduced illiteracy.

sections.title: Bureau of Research and Special Subjects
sections.summary: Literacy rose from 21 percent in August 1945 to 71 percent in August 1947. Higher education grew from 19 to 26 schools and 3,039 to 19,241 students; adult schools reached 15,502.

sections.title: Special Activities
sections.summary: A sub-committee proposed reopening Korean schools in Japan with approved textbooks. A Personnel Ceiling Board cut the Department's table of organization from 177 to 143.

sections.title: Bureau of Administration
sections.summary: A 3,200,000 won budget request was cut to 2,200,000 won. 2,041 new classrooms were built, yet classes average 95 children; per-classroom cost was estimated at 710,000 won.

sections.title: Bureau of Common Schools
sections.summary: Curriculum workshops at Taegu and Seoul trained teachers to run provincial workshops. Plans included 10 English vacation institutes, and half of Seoul's middle schools had American volunteer English teachers.

sections.title: Bureau of Teachers' Training
sections.summary: The Bureau prepared a booklet on teaching United Nations facts and sent a draft Educators' Guide to Washington. A Chunju meeting drew 600 against 200 expected; a summer session could train 10,000 teachers.

sections.title: Bureau of Higher Education
sections.summary: Advisers helped develop Taegu Agriculture College's curriculum. A Seoul National University committee chose a model ward of about 30 beds, and 2,000 nursing ethics textbooks were printed.

sections.title: Bureau of Adult Education and Culture
sections.summary: The Bureau prepared a manuscript on the schools' responsibility in the 10 May election and submitted it to the Department of Public Information for publication.

sections.title: Bureau of Textbooks
sections.summary: 13,230,670 textbooks had been published since 15 August 1945, including 678,500 Grade 6 science copies in April. The first 7,000 English-language textbooks arrived.

sections.title: American Language Institute
sections.summary: The American Language Institute began a new term on 26 April; the middle school teachers' evening class will meet four times weekly. One thousand surplus library books from Inchon went to it and normal schools.

sections.title: Bureau of Vocational Education
sections.summary: The adviser prepared a supplementary budget for a Korean Bureau of Vocational Education. A Korean Home Economics Association was organised; Taegu and Kaesong trips found equipment shortages.

sections.title: Section 3: Culture
sections.summary: Arbor Day tree planting (100,000,000 trees), Hodge's gift of instruments to the Symphony Orchestra, music and dance events, a Night of Poets, broadcasting and the Olympic team.

sections.title: Arbor Day
sections.summary: On 5 April, Arbor Day, Military Governor Dean planted the first of 100,000,000 trees nationwide, five per person; 26,000 trees covering 19 acres were planted on Nam San with about 10,000 participants.

sections.title: Korea Symphony Orchestra
sections.summary: On 25 April Lt.-Gen. Hodge presented instruments from U.S. personnel to the Korea Symphony Orchestra, now 60 musicians. Lim Won-sik conducted the first Korean performance of Douglas Moore's Village Music.

sections.title: Music and Dances
sections.summary: Events included a 28-29 April election publicity program by Seoul pupils, the 22d symphony concert under Kim In-soo, a rain dance by farmers on Nam San, and a 17 April court music program for UNTCOK.

sections.title: Other Cultural Activities
sections.summary: About 10,000 viewed cherry blossoms at the Zoological Gardens on 11 April. A Night of Poets on 25 April supported Korean culture in Japan. Two stamps issued 10 April showed Independence Arch and the turtle ship.

sections.title: Korea Broadcasting System
sections.summary: The Korea Broadcasting System publicised the election, ran a 52-student radio class at Ewha College, recorded Korean songs for pressing in the United States, and made two remote opera broadcasts.

sections.title: Sports
sections.summary: Fifty-eight athletes were selected for the London Olympics. A 560,000-ticket lottery raised funds to $140,000, averting a 35-man cut. Suh Yun-bok won the Boston-memorial marathon on 18 April.

sections.title: Section 4: Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: Press focused on the election and the Pyongyang conference: riots, law enforcement, the amnesty of 3,140 offenders, and fear of Japan after the closure of Korean schools.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: The 10 May election and the 19-24 April Pyongyang Conference dominated the press. Koreans read the closing of Korean schools in Japan as a plot to re-enslave Korea; American authorities saw a communist scheme.

sections.title: Pyongyang Conference
sections.summary: Conference coverage filled most newspaper space early in April. Rightist reporters found liberties completely suppressed in Soviet-controlled North Korea, while leftist reporters found conditions perfect.

sections.title: Registration for Election
sections.summary: Hodge's 2 April secret-ballot statement was printed, the civil rights ordinance took effect 1 April and an amnesty freed 3,140 offenders. 52 of 13,455 centers were attacked; Kyeng Hyang Sin Mun reported 91.7 percent registered.

sections.title: Political Campaign
sections.summary: Rightist papers complained that independents made up 48 percent of 939 candidates for 200 seats. Dean's 8 April press conference denied charges about a High Commissioner, Bank of Chosun notes and land sales.

sections.title: Law Enforcement
sections.summary: A Fatherland Protection Group enlisted men aged 18 to 55 against election terrorism. The Supreme Court rejected American advisers' 3 April petition on police warrants; Chang Duk-soo's assassins' sentences were commuted 23 April.

sections.title: Riots and Disorders
sections.summary: Disturbances in the south continued, with violence on Cheju-do from 3-7 April. A police report cited 15 killed and 30 wounded; a 29 April report described 2,000 armed men in dugouts and martial law.

sections.title: Fear of Japan
sections.summary: Papers protested the 31 March closing of Korean schools in Japan as an attack on Korean culture, while printing Dean's statement that they were communist training centers. The press feared Japanese travel permits would revive militarism.

sections.title: Section 5: Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: Korean National Youth mobilized 67,475 members for Arbor Day, grew to 774,949 members, opened training centers, trained apprentices, and urged voting in the 10 May election.

sections.title: Community Service
sections.summary: On Arbor Day, 5 April, 67,475 members in nine provinces planted 3,451,300 trees in 1,086,880 working hours; 1,246,480 trees were planted in early 1948 versus 175,000 in 1947. 7,000 members cleaned Inchon.

sections.title: Membership and Training
sections.summary: KNY membership reached 774,949 on 30 April 1948, including 108,326 women, growing by over 3,000 daily; 1,000,000 was forecast by 30 June. Training centers rose to 62, and 36,599 leaders were trained.

sections.title: Vocational Training
sections.summary: KNY emphasized recruiting employed workers and training apprentices, with on-the-job classes in about six communication and transportation industries. At Yongdongpo, apprentices assembled prefabricated homes.

sections.title: Election Preparations
sections.summary: Thousands of KNY members urged neighbors to vote in the 10 May election without backing any candidate, held neighborhood sessions on suffrage, and distributed ballots and boxes where funds were lacking.

sections.title: Section 6: Women's Activities
sections.summary: The Women's Bureau's election education, the Women's Press, sewing aids, a YWCA feeding program ($57,000), Junior Red Cross, KNY women and profiles of professional women; blank pages follow.

sections.title: The Women's Bureau
sections.summary: The Bureau gave over 50 election speeches and toured provinces with the film The Peoples Choice. Its mothers' school averaged 80 attendees and 5,000 copies of New Homemaking were distributed.

sections.title: The Women's Press
sections.summary: The Women's Press, Korea's only women's newspaper, founded 21 April 1947 with 27 staff and 8,000 daily circulation, urged women to vote in its 8 April editorial, citing 15,000,000 eligible women.

sections.title: Sewing Aids
sections.summary: U.S. church women's groups sent several hundred dollars' worth of sewing aids, handed to Korean welfare agencies. A family newly arrived from Manchuria altered clothing supplied by LARA.

sections.title: Domestic Economy Science Association
sections.summary: Korea's first home economics association was organized in April by adviser Mrs. Lyda Heffron at Shangshin Girls' Middle School, Seoul, with 30 charter members; only Seoul is active.

sections.title: The YWCA
sections.summary: The National YWCA received $57,000 from American Overseas Aid for Adolescents and the UN Appeal for Children to feed 2,000 undernourished adolescents at three Seoul primary schools; Dr. Y.Y. Kim is examining physician.

sections.title: Junior Red Cross
sections.summary: The first Korean Junior Red Cross members were initiated at a Seoul ceremony in April. Its first project is health education, supported by 50,000 boxes of toilet articles from the American Junior Red Cross.

sections.title: Women of Korean National Youth
sections.summary: The KNY women's section under Kim Hyun Suk trains women for citizenship; 108,326 of 774,949 members were women. Training covers first aid, home nursing and child care; 121 graduated at Suwon.

sections.title: Professional Women
sections.summary: Profiles of the Koh sisters: Evelyn (Doshisha law degree, Michigan M.A.), Gladys (piano diploma) and Dr. Nan (M.D.). They ran the Chamawon settlement; Evelyn now heads the Women's Bureau, Gladys the Red Cross women's volunteers.
